DAILY_TIP_1: Avoid sipping sugary drinks over long periods of time.
DAILY_TIP_2: Limit your intake of foods with added sugars (e.g. sweetened beverages like bubble tea and fruit juices, sweetened biscuits, sweets, chocolates).
DAILY_TIP_3: If you must, consume sugary things (e.g. cakes, snacks and sugary drinks) together with your main meals rather than in between meals.
DAILY_TIP_4: Always ask for reduced sugar/no sugar options in your drink when possible e.g. Kopi O or Kopi C Siew Dai, Bubble tea with 30% or 0% sugar.
DAILY_TIP_5: Avoid sugar-sweetened snacks and drinks between meals. If you need to snack, try healthy options such as plain water, cheese, whole fresh fruits, vegetables, or unsweetened nuts.
DAILY_TIP_6: Consider brushing your teeth gently after meals, or rinse with plain drinking water after consuming sugary foods and beverages to wash away the sugar and acid produced.
DAILY_TIP_7: Avoid frequent consumption of acidic drinks such as citrus fruit juice or carbonated drinks to avoid dental erosion.
DAILY_TIP_8: Brushing before going to bed is crucial as our saliva flow reduces as we sleep, allowing the sugar and bacteria still in your mouth to work overnight to cause decay.
DAILY_TIP_9: Brush gently twice a day using a soft bristled toothbrush and fluoridated toothpaste containing at least 1000-1450 ppm fluoride, for at least 2 mins each time.
DAILY_TIP_10: Rinse your mouth with water or brush gently after eating or drinking to help remove food debris and sugar so the bacteria on your teeth have less to feed on.
DAILY_TIP_11: Working from home? Don’t forget to brush your teeth even if you are not meeting anyone!
DAILY_TIP_12: Brushing Well doesn't mean Brushing hard. In fact, brushing too hard can cause enamel loss and abrasion cavities. Brush gently, one or two teeth at a time.
DAILY_TIP_13: Myth: No pain = No decay. Fact: Decay starts small. By the time you notice a hole or feel pain, the decay is already at a late stage. Visit your dentist for regular checkups and to prevent the progression of decay.

GROUP_1_ADVICE_INFO_ONE: The WHO recommends a maximum intake of 50g of sugar (~10 teaspoons) per day. The average Singaporean consumes 60 g of sugar a day, of which more than half come from beverages!
GROUP_1_ADVICE_INFO_TWO: Frequent consumption of sugar sweetened beverages increases your risk of decay, and your risk of diabetes.
GROUP_1_ADVICE_INFO_THREE: Bacteria in your mouth readily use the sugars in drinks to form acid which dissolve your teeth and cause decay
GROUP_1_ADVICE_INFO_FOUR: Although a drink label may say “No added sugar”, or “100% fruit juice” this does not mean that it’s better for your teeth. Regardless of whether the sugar is from natural sources or added, bacteria can utilize the free sugars in drinks to cause decay.
GROUP_1_ADVICE_INFO_FIVE: Myth: Natural sugars such as fructose in fruit juices, honey, and agave are healthy and will not cause decay. Fact: Bacteria in your mouth can use any type of sugar to cause decay.
GROUP_1_ADVICE_INFO_SIX: Drinking an additional 250 ml serving of sugar sweetened beverages every day increases your risk of diabetes by up to 26%
GROUP_1_ADVICE_INFO_SEVEN: Need caffeine? Many energy drinks have sugar content and more than half of SSB consumption is from caffeinated beverages. Choose caffeine sources with no sugar such as Oolong tea, Green tea or black coffee

FAQ_ONE_DETAIL: This app requires an internet connection (data plan or Wifi connection) to load information about your journaled dishes and for adding a new entry.
FAQ_TWO_DETAIL: This app is web-browser based with your data stored in cookies on your phone, thus clearing your cookies will also delete all entries. If you need to clear your cookies, try “Menu> Export” exporting the data first, you can then load the data later through the “Menu>Import” function.
FAQ_THREE_DETAIL: The diary page should contain all the dishes that you have logged previously. Try refreshing the web page, or reload the app to the latest version from the “Menu”. Note that your data is stored in web browser cookies so clearing your cookies will delete all entries.
FAQ_FOUR_DETAIL: You can check your journalled entries for the past weeks by tapping on the “Diary” tab and swiping left to view details on previous weeks. You can also swipe right to view the dates for the upcoming next weeks.
FAQ_FIVE_DETAIL_ONE: In the “Summary” report, the graph shows the total amount of sugar consumption (circles), and the number of meals consumed that day (bars) which are important dietary risk factors for caries development. (See “Content> Freq vs. Amount for more information). The “Intervals” graph illustrates the user’s dietary pattern with the traffic light dot system illustrating the amount of sugar consumed in that meal. This information will be useful for your dentist to provide appropriate and tailored dietary advice for you.
ABOUT_TEXT_PART_ONE: Food(lg) is a food journaling, nutrition tracking and analysis app on your diet, by simply taking pictures of what you have eaten. Powered by a deep-learning framework that learns the food type from image ‘pixels’, and based on standard nutritional guidelines and food composition data from the Health Promotion Board (HPB), Food(lg) calculates your daily nutrient estimates with the journaled entries for achieving a well-balanced diet.
ABOUT_TEXT_PART_TWO: This dental version of the Food(lg) expands the photo recognition capabilities of the original Food(lg) to focus on common high sugar items such as sugar sweetened beverages that increase the risk of decay. The aim of this app is to help patients keep track of their dietary patterns and raise awareness of the key dietary risk factors for caries e.g sugar consumption, cariogenicity of foods, and frequency of meals. Dental specific reporting features such as the sugar meter, frequency of meals, and custom dental advice regarding the foods consumed have been created.
ABOUT_TEXT_PART_THREE: The app is a collaborative research project by the Smart Systems Institute (SSI), the School of Computing Database Research Lab & the Faculty of Dentistry, from the National University of Singapore.

TUTORIAL_CONTENT_ONE: Learn more about how sugar affects your teeth and other dental tips to keep your teeth healthy!
CONTENT_DENTAL_DECAY_PART_ONE: Tooth decay (otherwise known as dental caries or cavities ) is damage to the tooth caused by bacteria in the mouth using sugar in your diet to form acid which then destroys the minerals in your tooth. Over time, this dissolution of minerals forms a permanent cavitation.
CONTENT_DENTAL_DECAY_PART_TWO: Therefore, decay is caused by: Bacteria + Sugar + Time = Decay, and the key to reducing your risk for dental decay lies in reducing your amount and frequency of sugar intake (thus starving the bacteria!), and removing the bacteria from your mouth through brushing at least twice a day with fluoride toothpaste.

CONTENT_SUGAR_MAIN_HEADER: Reducing the amount of sugar AND frequency of sugar intake
CONTENT_SUGAR_AMOUNT_PART_ONE: Health benefits of lower sugar intake in addition to less dental decay include lower risk of obesity, diabetes, heart disease and other health problems. The WHO recommends adults and children reduce their daily intake of free sugars to less than 10% of their total energy intake, and a further reduction to below 5% would provide additional health benefits.
CONTENT_SUGAR_AMOUNT_PART_TWO: Based on a 2,000-daily calorie intake, this would mean no more than 50g (or 10 teaspoons where 1 teaspoon is approximately 5g) or 25g of sugar (~5 teaspoons) per day for most adults. For context, a regular kopi already contains 20g (4 teaspoons) of sugar and mee siam can contain up to 50g (10 teaspoons) of sugar per serving!
CONTENT_SUGAR_AMOUNT_PART_THREE: Keeping track of your diet and the sugar you consume using this app, and making healthier choices every time can help reduce the amount of sugar you consume.
CONTENT_SUGAR_AMOUNT_HEALTHHUB_LINK_TEXT: To find out more about how to reduce your intake of sugar, read the article from
CONTENT_SUGAR_FREQUENCY_PART_ONE: A less well known fact about sugar is the effect that the frequency of sugar intake on the risk of dental decay.
CONTENT_SUGAR_FREQUENCY_PART_TWO: For example, drinking a 500 ml bottle of milk tea spread out over the whole day is worse for your teeth than drinking the whole bottle in one sitting. Although the total amount of sugar consumed is the same, intermittent sipping exposes your teeth repeatedly to the fermentable carbohydrates and sugar which bacteria metabolise to form acid, and results in many dips below the critical pH of 5.5* leading to damage to the tooth.
CONTENT_SUGAR_FREQUENCY_PART_THREE: *The critical pH is the pH at which the tooth enamel starts to dissolve and the minerals in the tooth move out of the crystalline structure of the tooth.
CONTENT_SUGAR_FREQUENCY_PART_FOUR: Within minutes of intake of fermentable carbohydrates, bacteria in the dental plaque on the tooth quickly metabolise the sugars to form acid, bringing the pH surrounding the tooth to below 5.5 where the minerals in the tooth start to dissolve out. Over time, saliva and fluoride in the saliva help bring the pH back up above 5.5 but if you consume another item with sugar or fermentable carbohydrates, the pH goes back down before the saliva can help remineralise the tooth.
CONTENT_SUGAR_FREQUENCY_PART_FIVE: The ‘Stephan curves’ below illustrate what happens in your mouth each time you eat. The food items were chosen for an average Singaporean adult. In the first example, foods containing sugars are consumed frequently, with little time in between for recovery to above the critical pH.
CONTENT_SUGAR_FREQUENCY_PART_SIX: The second example shows less sugar attacks, healthier food choices with no to low sugar, and more time in between meals for the teeth to be remineralised. We should all be aiming for this pattern with no more than 3 to 4 daily “acid attacks” from meals/snacks or drinks, low sugar foods, and plenty of time for the saliva to repair the damage done by eating sugar.
CONTENT_SUGAR_FREQUENCY_PART_SEVEN: Therefore, in addition to reducing the amount of sugary foods you consume, minimise snacking (even a small sip of a drink with sugar or a piece of sugar coated almond counts) and reduce the number of meals in a day to no more than 3-4 meals a day.
CONTENT_SUGAR_FREQUENCY_PART_EIGHT: If you must eat foods high in sugar, eat them over short periods of time or together with your main meals to minimise the time spent under the critical pH 5.5.
CONTENT_SUGAR_FREQUENCY_PART_NINE: Avoid eating or sipping sugary foods and drinks over long periods of time, and rinse your mouth with water after eating  to wash away the food debris, sugars, and neutralise the acids formed.

CONTENT_WAR_AGAINST_SUGAR_HEADER: The war against sugar sweetened beverages
CONTENT_WAR_AGAINST_SUGAR_PART_ONE: “On average, Singaporeans consumed twelve teaspoons (or 60g) of sugar daily. More than half of this came from sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs), of which 64 per cent were pre-packaged SSBs. This is a concern as drinking an additional 250 ml serving of SSB every day increases the risk of diabetes by up to 26%.”
CONTENT_WAR_AGAINST_SUGAR_PART_TWO: Frequent consumption of sugar sweetened beverages increases your risk of decay, and your risk of diabetes.The Health Promotion Board recommends keeping sugar intake to no more than 10% of our daily energy intake. That works out to be about 10 teaspoons of sugar per day for adults.
CONTENT_WAR_AGAINST_SUGAR_PART_THREE: Although a drink label may say “No added sugar”, or “100% fruit juice” this does not mean that it’s good for the teeth! This is because regardless of whether the sugar is from natural sources or added, bacteria can utilize the free sugars in drinks to cause decay. This is true for all drinks and fruit juices, even those labelled “no added sugar”, “100% fruit juice”, freshly squeezed juice from your favorite fruit store, or cold-pressed juice.
CONTENT_WAR_AGAINST_SUGAR_PART_FOUR: Similarly, while fruit juices contain many nutrients, they are also concentrated sources of natural sugars as many more fruits than you would normally consume as whole fruit are used to make up one cup of fruit juice. Therefore the total amount of sugar in fruit juices is high. In addition, in liquid form the sugar is more easily taken up by the bacteria on your teeth, causing decay.
CONTENT_WAR_AGAINST_SUGAR_ARTICLE_LINK_T: For more information about sugar in drinks, read the below articles:

CONTENT_DENTAL_EROSION_PART_ONE: Dental erosion refers to the dissolution of your tooth surface due to exposure to acids in your diet or from acid reflux/vomiting. Unlike dental decay, bacteria is not involved, but the wearing away of your tooth and the complex dental treatment such as fillings, crowns and even root canal treatment may be required if the condition is severe.
CONTENT_DENTAL_EROSION_PART_TWO: Common acidic foods and drinks include:
CONTENT_DENTAL_EROSION_PART_THREE: Reduce your consumption of acidic foods and drinks if you can or have these only at mealtimes. Other tips to prevent or stop erosion include:
CONTENT_DENTAL_EROSION_PART_THREE_FOOD_T: Citrus fruit juices such as orange, pineapple, and grapefruit juice
CONTENT_DENTAL_EROSION_PART_THREE_FOOD_F: Fizzy carbonated drinks such as sodas even if zero sugar
CONTENT_DENTAL_EROSION_PART_THREE_FOOD_S: Sour plum and other preserved dried fruits
CONTENT_DENTAL_EROSION_PART_FOUR: Reduce your consumption of acidic foods and drinks if you can or have these only at mealtimes. Other tips to prevent or stop erosion include:
CONTENT_DENTAL_EROSION_PART_FOUR_TIP_ONE: Eat whole fruits rather than fruit juices
CONTENT_DENTAL_EROSION_PART_FOUR_TIP_TWO: Avoid swishing or holding the acidic liquid in your mouth
CONTENT_DENTAL_EROSION_PART_FOUR_TIP_THR: Using a straw to drink acidic beverages (placing the straw behind your front teeth rather than in front and sucking the liquid through your teeth)
CONTENT_DENTAL_EROSION_PART_FOUR_TIP_FOU: Rinse your mouth with water or milk after consuming eating/drinking acidic foods.
CONTENT_DENTAL_EROSION_PART_FOUR_TIP_FIV: Rinse with fluoride mouthwash or sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) mouth rinse (one teaspoon of baking soda in a glass of water)
CONTENT_DENTAL_EROSION_PART_FOUR_TIP_SIX: Chewing sugar free dental chewing gum (available from pharmacies in Singapore) to increase saliva flow which will help raise the pH in your mouth
CONTENT_DENTAL_EROSION_PART_FOUR_TIP_SEV: Wait at least 1 hour after eating very acidic food/drinks or vomiting, to allow the minerals in your teeth to reform before brushing with a soft toothbrush.
CONTENT_DENTAL_EROSION_FIND_OUT_MORE_HEA: To find out more about dental erosion:
CONTENT_DENTAL_EROSION_FIND_OUT_MORE_LIN: Where Does the Acid That Causes Dental Erosion Come From?
CONTENT_TIPS_ONE: Reduce your frequency of meals and snacks.
CONTENT_TIPS_ONE_PART_ONE: Every snack, no matter how small (e.g. just one piece of candy) drops the pH in your mouth and provides the bacteria in your mouth with sugar to produce acid to dissolve your tooth.
CONTENT_TIPS_ONE_PART_TWO: Aim for a maximum of 3 meals a day
CONTENT_TIPS_TWO: Keep your sugar intake to below 50g of sugar per day and optimally, below 25g a day. (Ie 10 teaspoons and 5 teaspoons, respectively)
CONTENT_TIPS_THREE: Avoid sipping on sugary drinks over long periods of time.
CONTENT_TIPS_FOUR: Brush gently for at least 2 mins to remove the bacteria in your mouth.
CONTENT_TIPS_FIVE: Use fluoridated toothpaste. - Fluoride helps prevent the demineralisation of your tooth, speeds up the remineralisation of the tooth after an acid attack
CONTENT_TIPS_SIX: Myth: Brushing hard = Brushing well. Fact: Brushing too hard can cause enamel erosion and abrasion cavities.” Watch this video for how to brush gently and effectively.
CONTENT_TIPS_SEVEN: Myth: Rinsing with mouthwash can replace flossing or brushing. Fact: Mouthwash only comes into contact with the surface of the dental plaque and does not remove it.
CONTENT_TIPS_EIGHT: Myth: No pain = No decay. Fact: Decay starts small and then grows bigger. By the time you notice a hole or feel pain, the decay is already at a late stage. Visit your dentist regularly for checkups.
CONTENT_HIDDEN_SUGARS_PART_ONE: Many seemingly healthy foods and drinks contain high amounts of sugar. For example, sports drinks, flavored milk and yoghurts, and granola bars are some common culprits.
CONTENT_HIDDEN_SUGARS_PART_TWO: In terms of food, many packaged foods declaring “No fats” have high sugar instead to create flavour, and hawker foods such as mee siam and black carrot cake, actually contain more sugar than you would think.

FAQ_SIX_DETAIL_OLD: You can check your journaled entries for the past weeks by tapping on Diary (#2) tab and swiping left to view details on previous weeks. You can also swipe right to view the dates for next weeks for planning your diet. Alternatively, you can also tap on the “Diary” header to select dates from the calendar.
FAQ_SEVEN_DETAIL_OLD: The nutrition colored information can be changed by tapping on Profile (#5) tab and tap on 'SET NUTRITION TYPE' button. You can only select up to 6 different nutrition types including energy.
